newsitem.title: INDIA: India names recipients of Sweden's Bofors payments.
newsitem.headline: India names recipients of Sweden's Bofors payments.

text.p: Indian investigators on Tuesday released the names of five people they said had received payments from Swedish arms manufacturer Bofors in connection with a $1.3 billion artillery contract in 1986.
A statement from India's Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) said: "In connection with investigation in (the Bofors case) the first set of documents have been received from the Swiss authorities.

"The scrutiny of these documents reveal the following as the recipients of payments from the Bofors Company: 1. Mr. Ottavio Quattrochi and his wife Mrs Maria Quattrocchi; 2. Mr. Win Chadha and his wife Mrs. Kanta Chadha and his son Mr. W.H.Chadha."
The statement said: "The CBI is taking necessary steps to take action against the persons involved." It did not elaborate.
CBI spokesman S.M. Khan told Reuters by telephone: "We are only saying that payments were received. We have to see what is the nature of these payments." He did not elaborate.
Khan also said: "Mrs Chadha is dead. Her liability is no more."
Quattrocchi was the Indian representative of Italian engineering firm Snamprogetti SPA when the $1.3 billion artillery contract between Bofors AB and the Indian government was signed in 1986.
Neither Bofors nor Snamprogetti officials were immediately available for comment.
Chadha was the Indian agent for Bofors AB.
Swiss police have said there was evidence Bofors paid about $40 million into various banks accounts in Switzerland during the time the contract with India was drawn up and settled.
Bofors has denied the payments were bribes and said the money was settlement costs to its agents.

The Press Trust of India (PTI) news agency quoted Chadha, who now lives in Dubai, as saying: "I have already stated clearly before the authorities that I have neither given nor received any bribes throughout my life.

"I have offered time and again to the government of India including the CBI and former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao that I am ready and willing to depose before the government and give my statement and be interrogated in Dubai because my health does not permit me to travel."
After seven years of legal wrangling, Switzerland on January 21 released documents to the CBI about Swiss bank accounts that were allegedly linked to the artillery deal.
CBI Director Joginder Singh said then that the papers would allow India to begin digging into the case.
CBI spokesman Khan told Reuters: "Proceedings are going on in Switzerland. It may lead to more documents."
The furore over the alleged payments contributed to the defeat in 1989 of the government led by late prime minister Rajiv Gandhi, who was accused of involvement in the affair.
Gandhi, who denied the allegations, was killed in a bomb blast while campaigning for 1991 parliamentary polls.

Swiss investigator Michel-Andre Fels from the Federal Office for Police Affairs told reporters in Berne on January 21 that most of the papers handed over to Indian authorities were from banks in Geneva.
India has been trying to discover whether leading Indian politicians took bribes in connection with the arms deal.
